units.sentence: All high school students, public and private, can't use, hold or wear phones or similar devices from the first bell to the last
units.evidence_span: no public school student in grades nine through 12 shall be permitted to access personal electronic devices during the school day
units.problem: Scope error. P-007 covers only 'public school student[s] in grades nine through 12', and the bill title (P-001) is limited to 'local school systems and public schools'. No passage applies the rule to private schools, so 'public and private' is wrong. The parts drawn from P-003 (use, hold, wear) and P-002 (first bell to last, breaks, transitions) are accurate. 'All' also skips the plan-based exception (P-013) and students learning remotely (P-005).
units.suggested_fix: Public high school students can't use, hold or wear phones or similar devices from the first bell to the last, including breaks and time between classes, with narrow exceptions.

units.sentence: Students in public high schools, their families, and the school staff who enforce the rules.
units.evidence_span: assigning designated school personnel to oversee implementation and adherence to such policies and procedures
units.problem: Minor: 'their families' is not named in P-007 or P-014; P-011 or P-015 (parents and guardians) would support that part.
units.suggested_fix: Add P-011 or P-015 to the citation.

units.sentence: Schools must start on July 1, 2027.
units.evidence_span: Beginning no later than July 1, 2027
units.problem: Timing word changed. P-007 sets a deadline ('Beginning no later than July 1, 2027'), not a fixed start date. 'Start on' implies schools may not start earlier, but P-054 shows Cairo High School starting in 2026-2027. The document's own line 29 says 'no later than'.
units.suggested_fix: Schools must start no later than July 1, 2027. [P-007]

units.sentence: Each district sets details like phone storage and how parents reach students.
units.evidence_span: Establish appropriate methods for storing students' personal electronic devices
units.problem: Minor: the state, not the district, sets the core of how parents reach students (P-011(B): parents must contact the school directly). Districts set the protocol details.

units.sentence: That is where families can still have a say.
units.marker: {analysis: the state decision is final; districts adopt and revise their own policies each year under P-008}
units.problem: The reasoning holds: under P-008, each system adopts its policies, 'and revise[s] as appropriate', by January 1 each year, so the details are still open at the local level. Minor points: P-008 says 'revise as appropriate', not revise every year. No passage sets up a process for public input. 'The state decision is final' overstates, since the legislature can amend the law.
units.suggested_fix: Tag wording: 'districts adopt, and revise as appropriate, their own policies by January 1 each year (P-008)'.

Harrell says bans have 'been done in high schools already' (P-046), so early-adopter data could exist. The real basis is that none was found.

units.sentence: The same study found that mental well-being got worse.

P-043: 'There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with ... better mental wellbeing'. The study found no difference, not a decline. Because the study was cross-sectional (P-041), it couldn't show that anything 'got' worse over time anyway.
units.suggested_fix: The same study found no evidence that students at schools with strict rules had better mental well-being. [P-042, P-043]

And because this is a checkable factual claim, {editorial} is the wrong tag.

framing_issues.text: Breaking the rules leads to harsh, escalating consequences
framing_issues.issue: 'Harsh' is a side-taking adjective that isn't in P-012, which calls for 'progressive consequences' starting with verbal warnings. It casts the law's enforcement in a negative light inside a section meant only to describe what the law says.

framing_issues.text: The bill's sponsor, Rep. Scott Hilton, claimed
framing_issues.issue: Unequal verbs. Only the sponsor 'claimed'; every other speaker (Woods, Kemp, Adams, Harrell, the Emory epidemiologist) 'said'. The source (P-051) says 'Hilton said'. 'Claimed' signals doubt about one side's speaker.

framing_issues.text: How much focus, learning and well-being will improve in Georgia high schools
framing_issues.issue: Assumes the outcomes will improve, which is the supporters' premise, even though the evidence the document cites found no well-being benefit (P-042, P-043) and only second-year test gains (P-040).

framing_issues.text: An Emory epidemiologist said policies can address this with "rapid parent notification systems and guaranteed access to phones when needed."
framing_issues.issue: Selective quotation and placement. Only the rebuttal half of P-037 is quoted; the line before it ('Parents’ concerns about emergency access are valid and understandable') is left out, and argument 3's 'What supports it' cites no evidence at all. Putting the expert's recommendation under 'What the law says' may lead readers to think HB 1009 provides 'guaranteed access to phones when needed'. It doesn't: P-011 routes communication through the school.

framing_issues.text: What supports it: In the English study, students at schools with strict rules used phones about 60 minutes less
framing_issues.issue: Under the mental-health argument, 'What supports it' offers only a drop in phone use during school. That shows the rule changed behavior, not that mental health improved, and the same study found no well-being difference (P-042). Readers may take it as evidence of a mental-health benefit.

framing_issues.text: That is where families can still have a say.
framing_issues.issue: Together with the tag's 'the state decision is final', this tells readers the state-level question is closed. Laws can be amended, so this framing may discourage contacting legislators.
Generalizes from a single documented school (Cairo High School, P-054).
